title: The Pill

confidence.note: FDA records and the agency's own historians document the 1957 and 1960 approvals of Enovid. The facts of the Puerto Rico trials are not in dispute; how harshly to judge them by the standards of the 1950s is still argued.

place: Shrewsbury and Boston, Massachusetts; Río Piedras, Puerto Rico; Mexico City
people: Margaret Sanger (1879–1966), birth-control campaigner
Katharine McCormick (1875–1967), heiress who paid for the research
Gregory Pincus (1903–1967), biologist at the Worcester Foundation
John Rock, Catholic gynecologist who ran the clinical trials
Russell Marker, chemist who made progesterone from Mexican yams
Carl Djerassi (1923–2015), Syntex chemist whose group made norethindrone
Edris Rice-Wray, medical director of the Puerto Rico trials
summary: A pill for healthy women to take every day for years: built on Mexican yams, paid for by one heiress, tested on poor Puerto Rican women, and approved in 1960.
body: In 1960 the US Food and Drug Administration approved Enovid, a hormone pill made by G. D. Searle, as a contraceptive. The drug was already on sale. The FDA had cleared it in 1957 for menstrual disorders, and by late 1959 more than half a million American women were taking it, presumably most of them to avoid pregnancy. What was new in 1960 was the question regulators had to answer: whether a healthy woman could safely take a drug every day for years.

The chemistry came largely from Mexico. In 1942 the American chemist Russell Marker went looking for wild yams big enough to process and found the *cabeza de negro*, whose roots can weigh up to a hundred pounds. He turned its diosgenin into progesterone and in 1944 co-founded the company Syntex in Mexico City. Natural progesterone works poorly by mouth, and in 1951 Carl Djerassi's group at Syntex synthesized norethindrone, a potent oral version. Searle's chemists made a closely related compound, norethynodrel, which became Enovid.

The push to use these hormones for contraception came from two elderly women. Margaret Sanger, who had campaigned for birth control for four decades, met the biologist Gregory Pincus in 1951 and urged him to try. In 1953 the heiress Katharine McCormick wrote him a check for $40,000 and promised whatever else he needed. Pincus teamed up with John Rock, a Catholic Boston gynecologist, who began human tests on 50 women in Massachusetts under the cover of a fertility study, because the state's laws made contraception research all but impossible.

Larger trials began in April 1956 in a new housing project at Río Piedras, Puerto Rico. The medical director, Edris Rice-Wray, reported that the pill was 100% effective when taken properly but that 17% of the women complained of nausea, dizziness, headaches and vomiting, too many side reactions to be generally acceptable. Pincus and Rock dismissed her concerns. The women were told that the pill prevented pregnancy, not that it was experimental, and three deaths during the trials were never investigated.

The pill spread fast: by 1965 some 6.5 million American women were taking it. Its chief danger, blood clots, had not been anticipated by anyone, and proving the link took most of a decade. In 1970 the FDA made oral contraceptives the first drugs sold with a leaflet explaining risks to the patient, and doses have since been cut sharply.

links.note: The Pill was approved just before thalidomide changed drug regulation.
Consent rules on paper that the Puerto Rico trials barely met.
Rests on half a century of work on sex hormones.

title: Thalidomide

confidence.note: The drug's marketing, the 1961 identification by Lenz and McBride and its withdrawal are well documented. The figure of more than 10,000 affected children is a consensus estimate; miscarriages and stillbirths mean the true toll will never be known.

place: West Germany, Britain, Australia and worldwide; Washington, DC
people: Widukind Lenz, German clinician who linked the drug to birth defects
William McBride, Australian clinician who independently made the same link
Frances Oldham Kelsey, FDA medical officer
summary: A sleeping pill sold as harmless to pregnant women caused severe birth defects in more than 10,000 children, and forced the modern rules for testing drugs.
body: In the late 1950s the German firm Chemie Grünenthal began selling thalidomide as a sedative that was not addictive and, unlike barbiturates, would not kill in an overdose. It also eased nausea, and doctors gave it to pregnant women for morning sickness. Free sample packets went out to physicians to hand on. It became one of the world's best-selling drugs, advertised as completely safe.

It was not. Patients taking it developed nerve damage in their hands and feet, and reports came in of babies with rare and severe malformations, above all phocomelia, in which hands and feet project almost directly from the shoulders and hips. For years no one connected the two. In 1961 two clinicians working independently, Widukind Lenz in Germany and William McBride in Australia, identified thalidomide as the cause. It was withdrawn in Britain in November 1961 and from most of the world by 1962.

Between 1957 and 1962 the drug caused severe birth defects in more than 10,000 children. Up to 40% of the worst affected died in infancy, and many more pregnancies ended in miscarriage or stillbirth, so the true number will never be known. The disaster showed that animal species can react to a drug very differently from humans. No individual, and not Grünenthal itself, was ever successfully prosecuted.

The United States was largely spared because of Frances Kelsey, a pharmacologist and physician who joined the FDA in 1960. Thalidomide was one of the first applications she was given. Worried by the reports of nerve damage and by what the drug might do in pregnancy, she refused to approve it despite constant pressure from the company. Press coverage of her stand helped pass the Kefauver–Harris Drug Amendments of 1962, which for the first time required manufacturers to prove that a drug works, not just that it is safe, before selling it.

Thalidomide never went away. It is now used, under strict controls, to treat complications of leprosy and the blood cancer multiple myeloma. Where controls fail, as in Brazil, where leprosy is common, a new generation of children has been born with the same injuries.

title: Charnley's hip replacement

confidence.note: The November 1962 date comes from orthopedic histories rather than an original paper cited here; Charnley published the operation in stages from 1961. His central role in modern hip replacement is not disputed.

people: John Charnley (1911–1982), orthopedic surgeon
summary: A Lancashire surgeon worked out why artificial hips failed, and in 1962 settled on a design whose basic principles are still used.
body: Artificial hips existed before John Charnley, but they wore out, loosened and failed. Charnley, an orthopedic surgeon at Wrightington Hospital in England, treated the problem as one of engineering: friction. In 1956 he tried Teflon as a synthetic cartilage, but it wore away quickly and provoked intense tissue reactions. He switched to a tough, slippery polyethylene for the socket and fixed the parts to bone with acrylic cement. By November 1962 his low-friction arthroplasty had taken the form that made hip replacement routine.

title: Enders, Hilleman and the measles vaccine

confidence.note: US licensing dates for the measles vaccine (1963) and MMR (1971) are well documented. Credit for the first measles vaccine belongs mainly to Enders's group; Hilleman's contribution was the improved 1968 strain and the combined vaccine.

place: Boston, Massachusetts, and Merck & Co., United States
people: John Enders, virologist
Samuel L. Katz, Enders's colleague
Maurice Hilleman (1919–2005), vaccine scientist at Merck
summary: Measles virus taken from a sick schoolboy became a vaccine in 1963; Maurice Hilleman then made it gentler and folded it into MMR.
body: John Enders and Samuel Katz isolated measles virus from the blood of a 13-year-old boy, David Edmonston, and with colleagues weakened the "Edmonston strain" into a live vaccine licensed in the United States in 1963. At Merck, Maurice Hilleman produced a further attenuated version in 1968 that remains the main US measles vaccine, and in 1971 his combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, MMR, was licensed. Hilleman's team created more than 40 human and animal vaccines in all.

links.note: Enders's virus-culture methods also made the polio vaccines possible.
The combined vaccine later became the target of a fraudulent scare.

title: The modern hospice

confidence.note: The founding of St Christopher's in 1967 is well documented. Calling it the first modern hospice reflects its pairing of care with teaching and research; homes for the dying existed long before.

people: Cicely Saunders (1918–2005), nurse, social worker and physician
summary: A nurse turned doctor showed that dying patients could be kept awake and free of pain, and built a hospice in London to prove it.
body: Cicely Saunders trained as a nurse during the Second World War, then as a social worker, and qualified in medicine in 1957. In 1967 she opened St Christopher's Hospice in London, the first modern hospice to join care of the dying with teaching and research. Her key clinical change was giving opioids by mouth on a regular schedule, when most doctors believed they worked only by injection and caused addiction if given regularly. Her idea of "total pain", physical, psychological, social and spiritual, became a founding concept of palliative care.

links.note: The opposite answer to the new technologies of dying.

title: The first human heart transplant

confidence.note: The operation, the patients and their outcomes were documented in detail at the time. Barnard's surgical method was borrowed from experimental work at Stanford, a debt he did not hide.

place: Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town, South Africa
people: Christiaan Barnard, cardiac surgeon
Louis Washkansky, the recipient
Denise Darvall, the 25-year-old donor
Norman Shumway, Stanford surgeon who developed the technique in dogs
summary: A Cape Town surgeon put a young woman's heart into a dying man's chest. He lived 18 days, and the world's press followed nearly every hour.
body: In the early hours of 3 December 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town, Christiaan Barnard replaced the failing heart of Louis Washkansky with that of Denise Darvall, a 25-year-old woman certified brain-dead after a car accident; her father consented to the donation. Barnard's technique had been worked out in dogs by Norman Shumway's team at Stanford, and he had learned immunosuppression in Richmond, Virginia.

Washkansky died 18 days later. His doctors took his decline for rejection and increased his immunosuppressive drugs, but he had pneumonia, and the autopsy found no rejection at all. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, operated on 2 January 1968, lived for about 19 months. Most heart transplants attempted around the world over the next few years failed early.
The South African government, isolated by apartheid, quickly saw what the operation could do for the country's image. Barnard himself opposed racial segregation of patients in his department.

links.note: Kidney grafting pioneered the immunosuppression Barnard used.
Open-heart surgery made the operation possible.
Heart donation forced the question of when a ventilated patient is dead.

title: Redefining death

confidence.note: The 1959 French paper and the 1968 Harvard report are documented publications. How far the wish to obtain organs for transplantation drove the Harvard committee is still debated.

place: Paris, France; Harvard Medical School, Boston
people: Mollaret and Goulon, French physicians who described coma dépassé
Henry K. Beecher, chair of the Harvard committee
summary: Ventilators kept bodies alive after brains had stopped working. In 1968 a Harvard committee proposed that such patients were dead.
body: Mechanical ventilators created a state medicine had never seen: patients whose brains had stopped working but whose bodies could be kept going. In 1959 the French physicians Mollaret and Goulon called it *coma dépassé*, "a state beyond coma". In 1968 an ad hoc committee at Harvard Medical School, chaired by Henry Beecher, argued that irreversible coma should count as death, with criteria including absent brainstem reflexes, no spontaneous breathing and a flat EEG. The committee cited the burden on families and hospitals; brain death also eased organ transplantation, and how much that mattered is still debated.

links.note: Ventilators created the condition the committee had to define.
Transplant surgeons needed hearts from donors still on ventilators.

title: Oral rehydration therapy

confidence.note: The Dhaka and Calcutta trials of 1967–68 and Mahalanabis's work in 1971 are documented in published papers. Lives-saved totals, such as 70 million, are modeled estimates.

place: Dhaka (then East Pakistan) and Calcutta (Kolkata); refugee camps at Bangaon, India
people: David Nalin and Richard Cash, physicians at the Cholera Research Laboratory, Dhaka
Nathaniel F. Pierce, leader of the Johns Hopkins team in Calcutta
Dilip Mahalanabis (1934–2022), Indian pediatrician
summary: Salt, sugar and water by mouth: proved in cholera wards in 1968, then tested in a refugee crisis in 1971, it went on to save millions of lives.
body: Cholera kills by draining the body of water and salt, and the standard treatment was intravenous fluid. Laboratory work in the 1950s and 1960s showed that the gut absorbs sodium together with glucose, even during severe diarrhea. In 1967–68 a Johns Hopkins team in Calcutta led by Nathaniel Pierce, and David Nalin, Richard Cash and colleagues at the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka, showed that a glucose and salt solution given by mouth could replace most intravenous fluid; in Dhaka it cut IV needs by 80%.

The real test came in 1971, during the Bangladesh War of Independence. At refugee camps around Bangaon, India, the population reached about 350,000 by mid-June, with some 6,000 new cholera cases a day, and intravenous saline ran out. Dilip Mahalanabis had the oral solution given on a mass scale, much of it by family members, and deaths fell.

*The Lancet* later called oral rehydration "potentially the most important medical advance" of the century; that qualifying word is often dropped. One recent estimate credits it with about 70 million lives.

links.note: Snow found how cholera spreads; ORS gave a cheap way to survive it.
A model of the cheap, community-delivered care Alma-Ata promoted.
